title: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.2 Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions
intro: After this lesson you can describe the center, spread and shape of the sampling distribution of $\hat p$, check the conditions with numbers, and use the normal model to find probabilities.

moments.title: Sampling distribution of $\hat p$
moments.text: The distribution of all possible sample proportions from all possible samples of one size from one population.

moments.title: One $p$, many $\hat p$
moments.text: A population has one proportion but every sample has its own, so $\hat p$ is a random variable.

moments.title: Peanut allergy
moments.text: $p=0.17$ and samples of 140 people. Samples of 25, 32 and 27 allergic people give 17.9%, 22.9% and 19.3%.

moments.title: Three characteristics, three conditions
moments.text: Describe the center, spread and shape, and check the condition that goes with each.

moments.title: Center
moments.text: $\mu_{\hat p}=p$, provided the samples are random.

moments.title: Independence and the 10% condition
moments.text: Sampling without replacement is fine when $n$ is at most 10% of the population.

moments.title: Shape
moments.text: The sampling distribution is approximately normal when the sample is big enough.

moments.title: Normality condition
moments.text: Expect at least 10 successes and 10 failures: $np\ge10$ and $n(1-p)\ge10$.

moments.title: Streaming documentaries
moments.text: 27% of subscribers watch a documentary weekly. For $n=600$: center 0.27, SD about 0.0181, approximately normal.

moments.title: Bigger samples vary less
moments.text: Changing $n$ from 600 to 2,000 leaves the center at 0.27 but shrinks the SD to about 0.0099.

moments.title: $P(\hat p>0.30)$
moments.text: Find $z$ for 0.30, then use the standard normal distribution. The answer is about 0.049.

moments.title: Normal probabilities in Desmos
moments.text: Plus, Inference, Probability Distributions, Normal with mean 0 and SD 1, then Cumulative Probability.

moments.title: Commuters and public transit
moments.text: $p=0.18$ and $n=1000$ give SD about 0.0121. About 90% of samples land between 16% and 20%.

moments.title: Cutoffs for the most extreme 5%
moments.text: Split 5% into 2.5% in each tail and find the $z$-scores that mark them.

moments.title: Turn $z$ back into $\hat p$
moments.text: Solve $\pm1.96=\dfrac{\hat p-0.65}{0.0238}$ to get about 0.603 and 0.697.

moments.title: Build the model with no sample at all
moments.text: All you need is $p$ and $n$ to show what every sample proportion could look like.

sections.title: Can I use a normal model for $\hat p$?

cards.name: Center
cards.text: $\mu_{\hat p}=p$ when the sample is random.

cards.name: Spread
cards.text: $\sigma_{\hat p}=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ when $n$ is at most 10% of the population.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: When you describe a sampling distribution, give each condition with its numbers, for example $600(0.27)=162\ge10$ and $600(0.73)=438\ge10$. A phrase like "the conditions are met" earns less credit.

sections.title: Describe the sampling distribution of $\hat p$
sections.intro: Six items earn the credit: center, spread and shape, each with its condition. You need only $p$ and $n$, not a sample.
steps: Center: $\mu_{\hat p}=p$. Condition: the samples are random.
Spread: $\sigma_{\hat p}=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. Condition: $n$ is at most 10% of the population, which you assume when the population size is unknown.
Shape: approximately normal. Condition: $np\ge10$ and $n(1-p)\ge10$, computed with $p$.
To find a probability, convert $\hat p$ to $z=\dfrac{\hat p-p}{\sigma_{\hat p}}$ and use the standard normal distribution.

parts.label: Spread
parts.text: How far sample proportions typically sit from 0.27.

parts.label: Shape
parts.text: Both at least 10, so the model is approximately normal.

sections.title: Sampling distribution explorer
sections.intro: Set $n$ and $p$, then take 1,000 samples. The histogram is built from simulated sample proportions and the curve is the model from this lesson. Watch the spread shrink as $n$ grows while the center stays at $p$.

stories.stream: 27% of a streaming service's subscribers watch at least one documentary a week. Each sample is 600 randomly chosen subscribers.
stories.comm: 18% of a city's commuters use public transit. Each sample is 1,000 randomly chosen commuters.
stories.camp: 54% of first-year students at a university live on campus. Each sample is 250 randomly chosen students.
stories.poll: 65% of adults support stricter rules for social media. Each sample is 400 randomly chosen adults.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Work through each task in it yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Right-tail probability
steps.suppose: we want $P(\hat p>0.30)$ for the streaming service: $p=0.27$, $n=600$.
steps.how: find $z$ by typing (0.30-0.27)/sqrt(0.27*0.73/600) on a new line. Then tap the plus button, choose Inference, then Probability Distributions, then Normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Open Cumulative Probability, choose the right option and enter your $z$.
steps.observe: Only a small sliver on the right is shaded. Open the dropdown for more decimals.

steps.title: Between two values
steps.suppose: we want the chance that a sample of 1,000 commuters has $\hat p$ between 0.16 and 0.20, with $p=0.18$.
steps.how: find the standard deviation with sqrt(0.18*0.82/1000), then $z=\pm0.02/\text{SD}$. In Cumulative Probability choose the inner option and enter the two $z$-scores.
steps.observe: The shaded area is the large central chunk. The two $z$-scores are the same size with opposite signs because 0.16 and 0.20 are equally far from 0.18.

steps.title: Left-tail probability
steps.suppose: we want $P(\hat p\le0.50)$ for campus housing: $p=0.54$, $n=250$.
steps.how: find $z$ for 0.50, then in Cumulative Probability choose the left option and enter it.
steps.observe: The shaded tail is on the left because "at most" points down. Whether you use $<$ or $\le$ makes no difference for a continuous model.

steps.title: Cutoffs for the most extreme 5%
steps.suppose: we want the values of $\hat p$ that bound the most extreme 5% for $p=0.65$, $n=400$.
steps.how: in Cumulative Probability switch from area to bounds, choose the inner option and enter 0.95 to get $z^*$. Then type 0.65-1.96*sqrt(0.65*0.35/400) and 0.65+1.96*sqrt(0.65*0.35/400) on new lines.
steps.observe: The bounds are symmetric because the normal model is. Sample proportions outside the two cutoffs are the unusual ones.

steps.title: Effect of sample size
steps.suppose: we want to compare the spread for $n=600$ and $n=2000$ when $p=0.27$.
steps.how: type sqrt(0.27*0.73/600) and sqrt(0.27*0.73/2000) on separate lines.
steps.observe: The center is 0.27 in both cases. Only the standard deviation changes, and the larger sample has the smaller one.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Describing the center
traps.better: The mean of the sampling distribution of $\hat p$ is $\mu_{\hat p}=0.27$, because the samples are random, so $\hat p$ is an unbiased estimator of $p$.

traps.title: Checking conditions without numbers
traps.weak: The conditions are met, so the model is normal.
traps.better: Random: the sample was random. 10%: 600 is less than 10% of all subscribers. Large counts: $600(0.27)=162\ge10$ and $600(0.73)=438\ge10$.

traps.title: Interpreting the standard deviation
traps.weak: 0.0181 is the standard deviation of the 600 subscribers.
traps.better: In samples of 600 subscribers, the sample proportion typically varies by about 0.0181 from the population proportion 0.27.

traps.title: Writing a probability in context
traps.better: $P(\hat p>0.30)\approx0.049$: about a 4.9% chance that a random sample of 600 subscribers has more than 30% who watch a documentary weekly.

traps.title: Saying a larger sample moves the center
traps.weak: With $n=2000$ the mean of $\hat p$ gets closer to 0.27.
traps.better: The center stays at $\mu_{\hat p}=0.27$ for every $n$. A larger $n$ shrinks the standard deviation from about 0.0181 to about 0.0099.

questions.stem: A population has $p=0.40$. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat p$ for random samples of size 250?
why: This is the variance-style value $0.40(0.60)/250$ with the square root left off.
This leaves out the factor $(1-p)$ under the square root.
This divides by $\sqrt{250}$ instead of taking the square root of the whole fraction.

questions.stem: Which condition makes the formula $\sigma_{\hat p}=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ appropriate?
opts: The sample is at most 10% of the population
why: Random sampling is what makes the center equal $p$.
This is the 10% condition, which supports independence and so the spread formula.
These counts make the shape approximately normal.
$n\ge30$ belongs to sampling distributions of means, not to this formula.

questions.stem: The sample size is multiplied by 4 and $p$ stays the same. What happens to the standard deviation of $\hat p$?
why: $n$ sits under a square root in the denominator, so the SD does not grow with $n$.
The SD gets smaller, not larger.
$\sqrt{4}=2$ and $n$ is in the denominator, so the SD is cut in half.
The center is unchanged, but the spread depends on $n$.

questions.stem: For $p=0.30$ and $n=200$, which is closest to $P(\hat p\ge0.35)$?
why: $z=(0.35-0.30)/0.0324\approx1.543$, and the right-tail area is about 0.0614.
This is the area to the left of $z$, not the right tail.
This doubles the tail, which is for a two-sided question.
This is the value of $\hat p$, not a probability.

questions.stem: A rare trait has $p=0.04$ and random samples have $n=150$. Which statement is correct?
opts: The sampling distribution of $\hat p$ is approximately normal because $n>30$
The sampling distribution is approximately normal because the sample is random
A normal model is not appropriate because $np=6$ is less than 10
A normal model is not appropriate because $n$ is more than 10% of the population
why: $n>30$ is not the condition for proportions.
Random sampling does not guarantee a normal shape.
$150(0.04)=6<10$, so the expected number of successes is too small.
Nothing in the problem says $n$ is more than 10% of the population.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A school district reports that 22% of its 15,000 students ride the bus. A researcher plans to take a random sample of 400 students.
parts: (a) Describe the sampling distribution of $\hat p$, the sample proportion who ride the bus: give its center, spread and shape, and check the conditions.
(b) Find the probability that fewer than 20% of the sampled students ride the bus.
(c) Would a sample proportion of 0.30 be unusual? Justify your answer.
sample: (a) Center: $\mu_{\hat p}=0.22$, because the sample is random. Spread: $\sigma_{\hat p}=\sqrt{0.22(0.78)/400}\approx 0.0207$, and 400 is less than 10% of 15,000, which is 1,500. Shape: approximately normal, because $400(0.22)=88\ge10$ and $400(0.78)=312\ge10$.
(b) $z=\dfrac{0.20-0.22}{0.0207}\approx-0.966$, so $P(\hat p<0.20)\approx0.167$. About a 16.7% chance that fewer than 20% of the sampled students ride the bus.
(c) $z=\dfrac{0.30-0.22}{0.0207}\approx3.86$, which is more than 3 standard deviations above the mean. A sample proportion of 0.30 would be very unlikely if $p=0.22$, so it would be unusual.
checklist: (a) Spread about 0.0207 with the 10% condition checked against 1,500
(c) $z$ about 3.86 and a conclusion that 0.30 is unusual
